hero.title: DBT Skills: A Plain-English Guide
hero.lead:
Dialectical behavior therapy — DBT — is a skills-based therapy built for emotions that arrive fast and land hard. Rather than only talking about feelings, it teaches named skills you can reach for at 2am, when good intentions are not enough.

Here are the four modules in plain language, with one usable skill from each. This is an explainer, not a course — real DBT is delivered by trained therapists, as individual sessions plus a weekly skills group. On your own: learn the vocabulary, practice the simpler skills, and daily mood tracking to find which ones help you.

sections.heading: What DBT is — and what it isn't
sections.html:
Psychologist Marsha Linehan built DBT in the 1980s for intense emotional swings and self-harm urges; it now serves borderline personality disorder, eating disorders, substance use, chronic suicidality, and anyone whose emotions simply run hot.

Dialectical names the core idea: two opposite things can be true at once. You are doing the best you can, and you can learn to do differently.

The full program is four parts: weekly individual therapy, a skills group, phone coaching in the moment, and a consultation team for the therapists. An article is not that. If your emotions regularly overwhelm you, a referral to a DBT therapist is the step that changes things.

sections.heading: The four modules at a glance
sections.html:
Two modules accept reality as it is (mindfulness, distress tolerance); two change it (emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness). Mindfulness comes first — none of the others work if you can't notice what's happening in time to use them.

ModuleWhat it's forExample skillWhat that looks like
MindfulnessNoticing what you feel without immediately acting on itWise mindThe middle point between raw emotion and cold logic
Distress toleranceGetting through a crisis without making it worseTIPPCold, movement, breath — body chemistry over willpower
Emotion regulationMaking intense emotions hit less often and pass soonerOpposite actionThe opposite of what the emotion urges, done fully
Interpersonal effectivenessAsking and refusing without wrecking the relationship or your self-respectDEAR MANA seven-step script for the conversation you're dreading

sections.heading: Four skills, in detail
sections.html:
Wise mind (mindfulness)

DBT names three states: emotion mind, where feelings decide; reasonable mind, all facts and no warmth; and wise mind, the overlap where you know something calmly and completely. Pause, breathe, ask your question, and wait for the answer that feels settled rather than urgent — urgency is usually emotion mind talking.

TIPP (distress tolerance)

For distress at a nine or ten, TIPP skips reasoning and works on physiology: Temperature — cold water or a cold pack on the face; the dive reflex slows the heart. Intense exercise — a hard ten minutes. Paced breathing — out-breath longer than in-breath. Paired muscle relaxation — tense on the in-breath, release on the out. The cold and exercise skills change heart rate deliberately: check with your doctor first if you have a heart condition, an eating disorder, are pregnant, or take medication affecting heart rate. Several double as grounding techniques.

Opposite action (emotion regulation)

Every emotion carries an urge: fear says avoid, shame says hide, anger says attack. When the urge doesn't fit the facts, following it strengthens the emotion for next time. Check the facts, then do the opposite all the way — send the dreaded message, warmly; stay in the room; stand up straight.

DEAR MAN (interpersonal effectiveness)

A script for a conversation that matters: Describe the facts, Express how you feel, Assert what you want, Reinforce what the other person gains — then stay Mindful of your goal, Appear confident, Negotiate where you can. Companions GIVE and FAST protect the relationship and your self-respect.

sections.heading: The diary card: DBT's own tracking habit
sections.html:
The piece that makes the skills stick: the diary card. DBT clients fill one in daily — emotions rated, urges noted, skills used and whether they helped — and the session opens with the therapist reading the week, not asking "so, how have you been?"

Borrow it without a program. One entry a day: a rating, the factors in play, any urges, which skill you tried — and the field everyone skips, whether it helped. After a month that column is the surprise; almost nobody's list matches what they expected. The emotion wheel helps you name what you're rating first.

sections.heading: Paper diary card vs an app: an honest comparison
sections.html:
The printed card has a real case: free, works when your phone doesn't, and handwriting suits reflection. If your therapist wants the paper card, use the paper card.

Paper's weakness is the second month. Loose sheets never add up to anything you can look at, and the card is never in your pocket when the urge shows up. The app closes that gap: five-second logging, charts showing which factors travel with your worst days, reminders, notes and photos, and PDF, XLSX, CSV or JSON export — three months for your therapist instead of three days. Private by design: iCloud sync, no account, no email, optional Apple Health sync.

Feeltracker Mood & BPD is a self-monitoring tool, not therapy and not a diagnostic instrument — it doesn't score you or tell you what your ratings mean.

items.question: Can I learn DBT skills on my own?
items.answer: Many of them, yes — the skills are taught openly, and workbooks exist for exactly this reason. What you can't self-provide is the rest of the program: a therapist who knows your history, a group to practice with, coaching in the moment. Treat solo learning as a useful start, not a substitute for care if your emotions regularly overwhelm you.

items.question: What's the difference between DBT and CBT?
items.answer: DBT grew out of CBT and shares its practical, skills-first approach. CBT concentrates on examining and changing unhelpful thoughts; DBT adds a large **acceptance** half — distress tolerance, mindfulness, validation — alongside the change work, plus a defined skills curriculum and a group component.

items.question: Do I need a BPD diagnosis to use DBT skills?
items.answer: No. DBT was developed with borderline personality disorder in mind, but the skills are general-purpose emotional tools now used for many other difficulties — plenty of people with no diagnosis find TIPP and opposite action useful. If you're reading because something feels familiar, our guide to [BPD and mood tracking](/mood-journal/bpd-symptoms/) is a gentler place to start than a symptom checklist.

items.question: How long does a full DBT program take?
items.answer: A standard skills group runs through the four modules over roughly six months, and many programs recommend two full cycles — about a year, alongside weekly individual therapy. Shorter skills-only groups are increasingly common; your clinician will tell you what's realistic where you live.

items.question: What should I track between sessions?
items.answer: The traditional diary card: a daily mood rating, the factors around it, any urges, and which skills you used and whether they helped. Keep it small enough to survive a bad day — see [how to track your mood](/mood-journal/how-to-track-your-mood/) for a version that takes about five seconds.

data.disclaimerText: This article is for general information only — not therapy, medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Reading about DBT skills is not receiving DBT: the full program is delivered by trained clinicians. If your emotions regularly feel unmanageable, ask a doctor or mental health professional about a referral. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself or of suicide, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line in your country now — you deserve support in the moment, not in six weeks.
